text.p: The Irish pound came under fierce selling pressure in late trade on Wednesday on market talk that a major investment bank was about to release a negative report on the currency, dealers and analysts said.
"No report has yet been released but there are rumours in the market that a big investment bank is about to release a recommendation on the Irish pound," an economist in London said.
The talk sent the punt reeling -- by 1630 GMT it had plunged more than four pfennigs to 2.5566 marks from 2.6001 at Tuesday's close. It slumped to 0.9180 stg from 0.9326 and $1.5110 from $1.5346.
Dealers said the report was believed to say that the Irish pound would weaken towards its central Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) rate of 2.4111 marks as economic and monetary union (EMU) approached.
It was the second time in a month that the Irish pound had been sent into a spin because of a market belief that it must fall against the German currency before Ireland's EMU membership.

Three weeks ago the pound plunged against the mark in what dealers said was a reaction to the Irish finance minister's televised comments that he would like to see it closer to its central ERM values.
The Central Bank of Ireland was forced to raise interest rates by half a point on May 1 in a surprise move aimed at stemming the punt's fall.
Dealers said at the time that the punt's battering illustrated the kind of adjustments EU currencies would be expected to make to prepare for the launch of the single currency.
The Irish pound appreciated dramatically against the mark in the second half of 1996 and early 1997, lifted on the coat-tails of a resurgent sterling.

Sterling dragged the punt to the top of the ERM grid, prompting fears among some economists that the current punt/mark rate would be unsustainable in the long term and would be a disastrous rate to enter EMU.
On Tuesday, David Begg of Britain's Centre for Economic Policy Research said Ireland should join EMU at its central rate.
"Ireland...is the only likely (EMU) member facing a devaluation to get to its central rate," Begg said at the launch of a study on EMU in Dublin.
